description: FireRelay harmonizes 25 years of NASA FIRMS hotspots (MODIS 2000+, VIIRS 2012+) into one NOAA-20-equivalent record and a burning-activity calendar for any area on Earth, built with Singapore's transboundary haze season in mind.
summary: FireRelay turns 25 years of NASA FIRMS active-fire hotspots into one continuous record and a burning-activity calendar for any area on Earth. MODIS (since 2000, 1 km pixels) and VIIRS (since 2012, 375 m) count the same fires very differently: VIIRS records 6 to 12 times more hotspots. Stitched records therefore show a false jump in 2012, and S-NPP stopped delivering data on 2 November 2026. We calibrated 566 million detections, all passed through identical filters, into one unit: NOAA-20 VIIRS-equivalent hotspots. The record is handed on like a relay, MODIS to S-NPP to NOAA-20, using per-cell, per-calendar-month ratios shrunk toward regional values. On years the model never saw, yearly totals for named regions have a median error of 12% (raw MODIS: 88%), monthly totals for 1-degree blocks 34% (raw MODIS: 87%), and the record picks the same peak burning month 77% of the time. It beats quantile mapping and log-log regression on the same tests, and every area shows its own measured error. Users draw an area or pick a place and get a 2001 to 2026 monthly or weekly calendar, anomalies against the typical month, records, 80% uncertainty ranges and a CSV. The live data shows why this matters. Central Kalimantan, a haze source for Singapore, had 17 times its typical October in 2026, and 2026 is already its 3rd-worst fire year since 2001. Singapore's regional haze centre compares only the last 5 years; FireRelay compares 25.
details:
What FireRelay does

FireRelay is a free web tool (firerelay.vercel.app) that answers one question for any place on Earth: when does it burn, and how does this month compare with the last 25 years? You pick a place, draw a rectangle or polygon, or type coordinates. FireRelay then builds a burning-activity calendar from January 2001 to today from one harmonized record of NASA FIRMS hotspots. Each area also shows its own measured hold-out error, a naive stitch versus FireRelay trend check, and a typical next-three-months outlook from history (not a forecast). Haze Watch areas also show the latest week against a typical week and Singapore's live PM2.5 from NEA.

  • Monthly calendar (years by months) with a "Typical" row (median 2001 to 2025), year totals and record markers.
  • "vs typical month" view: each month as a multiple of that calendar month's median, using a colour-blind-safe diverging scale.
  • Weekly calendar (53 weeks by 26 years). It answers the challenge author's question of whether a weekly calendar can stay readable: one thin row per year, like a contribution graph.
  • Status cards: latest full month against typical (rank among all years), the partial current month, year to date against typical, and the typical burning season.
  • Map drill-down: click any month to see where it burned, cell by cell.
  • Honest provenance: months estimated from MODIS are hatched and carry an 80% uncertainty range, and partial months are dashed. Every tooltip shows the raw Terra, Aqua, S-NPP and NOAA-20 counts behind the number.
  • CSV download: units, source, partial-month flag, uncertainty bounds, raw counts per sensor, median, ratio and rank. Areas can be downloaded as GeoJSON, and every view has a shareable link.

Why harmonization is needed now

MODIS (Terra since 2000, Aqua since 2002) detects hotspots in 1 km pixels. VIIRS (S-NPP since 2012, NOAA-20 since 2018) uses 375 m pixels and finds many more, smaller fires. Worldwide, S-NPP VIIRS records about 6 times as many hotspots as Aqua MODIS and 12 times as many as Terra MODIS in the same months, measured from our own processing. Stacking the records creates a false explosion of fire in 2012, and using VIIRS alone throws away 11 years. The timing is pressing: FIRMS announced that S-NPP stopped delivering data on 2 November 2026, and MODIS is near the end of its life.

How it works

  1. Data. NASA FIRMS standard (science-quality) yearly archives: MODIS Collection 6.1 (Nov 2000 to 2025), VIIRS 375 m S-NPP (2012 to 2025) and NOAA-20 (Apr 2018 to 2025). 2026 comes from the FIRMS area API: standard data for January to July, near-real-time for August to 15 November. In total, 566 million detections were streamed and aggregated.
  2. Identical filters for every sensor. We keep presumed vegetation fires only (FIRMS type 0, which drops volcanoes, static industrial sources and offshore flares) and nominal or high confidence detections. Near-real-time files have no type flag, so we remove static sources cell by cell using each cell's 2025 static-source share.
  3. Gridding. Counts are made on a 0.25 degree grid by month (and a 1 degree grid by week). Terra and Aqua are kept separate because they pass at different times of day.
  4. Target unit: NOAA-20 VIIRS equivalent. NOAA-20 (and NOAA-21) carry the record forward, so every new month is an observation and needs no model. Operational agencies already count in it: the ASEAN Specialised Meteorological Centre in Singapore reports NOAA-20 hotspot counts. Choosing VIIRS also keeps its sensitivity to small agricultural and peat fires.
  5. The relay (calibration chain). From April 2018: observed NOAA-20. February 2012 to March 2018: S-NPP multiplied by a per-cell NOAA-20/S-NPP ratio (global value 0.99). Before February 2012: Terra and Aqua are each multiplied by a per-cell, per-calendar-month ratio fitted against S-NPP, and the two estimates are averaged. This also handles the Terra-only months of 2001 and 2002.
  6. Robust ratios. Each ratio is a ratio of sums, shrunk toward its parent (0.25 degree cell, then 1 degree block by calendar month, then 1 degree block, then 5 degree tile, then the globe) with a pseudo-count chosen on validation data. Busy cells get their own ratio; sparse cells borrow strength. The MODIS ratios are fitted on February 2012 to December 2019, while both MODIS platforms still held their designed orbits.

Validation on years the model never saw

  • Test A (train 2012 to 2016, test 2017 to 2019), median absolute error of monthly totals:
    Overall bias is under 1%. Correlation of log counts is 0.92 at 5 degrees. The calendar picks the same peak burning month as VIIRS in 77% of 21,438 region-years.
    • 0.25 degree cells: 39% for FireRelay, against 42% for one global ratio and 86% for raw MODIS.
    • 1 degree blocks: 34%, against 43% and 87%.
    • 5 degree tiles: 26%, against 38% and 89%.
  • Same tests, yearly totals: 14% for 1 degree blocks, 10% for 5 degree tiles and 12% for the 12 named areas in the app, against about 88% for raw MODIS. Whole-globe yearly totals are within 1%.
  • Method contest, same splits: at 1 degree monthly FireRelay 34%, one global ratio 43%, quantile mapping 48%, log-log regression 61%, raw MODIS 87%. Yearly 5 degree tiles: 10%, 26%, 106%, 134%, 88%.
  • Test B (train 2012 to 2019, test 2020 to 2025, with MODIS orbits drifting): still 37% at 1 degree.
  • Noise floor: the two VIIRS satellites, observing the same fires about 50 minutes apart, disagree by 17% at the same scale.
  • End-to-end spot check: October 2026 over Central Kalimantan: 78,472 hotspots in FireRelay against 79,630 counted directly in the FIRMS API (minus 1.5%).

The hold-out error distribution is also the uncertainty model: every estimated month gets an 80% range sized to its count. The first ranges were too narrow (76% coverage), so we widened them by one factor fitted on Test A; they now hold 80% of Test A and 77% of the unseen 2020 to 2025 drift years. Riau is overestimated in every hold-out year, so MODIS-era peatland months are the least certain part of the record.

Local impact: Singapore's haze season

Haze reaches Singapore from peat and plantation fires in Sumatra and Borneo. The regional haze centre in Singapore compares each month's hotspot counts with only the previous five years of NOAA-20 data. FireRelay puts the same units back to 2001. The live data is striking. Central Kalimantan had about 68,800 hotspots in October 2026, 17 times its typical October, and 2026 is already the province's 3rd-worst fire year since 2001, after 2006 and 2015 (the 2015 haze crisis), with six weeks still to go. Preset areas cover the main haze sources: Riau, Jambi and South Sumatra, West and Central Kalimantan, Peninsular Malaysia and Indonesia. Presets for Córdoba and Corrientes (Argentina), Pará (Brazil), New South Wales and California show that the method works anywhere.

Built to be used and to last

FireRelay is a static website: about 70 MB of compressed tiles, plain HTML and JavaScript, and a NASA GIBS Blue Marble basemap. There is no server, database or API key in the browser, so it keeps working through judging and beyond at no cost. The fire colour ramp runs from dark to light, so it reads by brightness alone, which works for colour-blind readers and in greyscale. A table view supports screen readers, and the calendar can be navigated with the keyboard. The full pipeline (Node.js, no native dependencies) can rebuild every number from the FIRMS archive with a few commands.

Limitations

Hotspots are detections, not burned area or emissions, and clouds and smoke hide fires. The MODIS-era estimate assumes the 2012 to 2019 relationship between sensors held earlier, which the 80% ranges only partly capture. Areas are built from 0.25 degree cells. The latest months are near-real-time data and may be revised slightly. FireRelay gives seasonal and historical context, not same-day tactical alerts.

What's next

Cross-calibrate NOAA-21 to NOAA-20 as a backup; refresh the data monthly with a scheduled job; work with haze and emergency centres (ASMC, CONAE) to add 25 years of context to their monthly reviews. The per-cell ratio tables are small enough to run on board a satellite as an app.

Links

App: firerelay.vercel.app · Method and validation: method.html · Source code: source · Demo video: 30 s video · Slides: 7-slide PDF

Tools: Node.js (data pipeline), plain HTML, CSS and JavaScript, Leaflet 1.9.4, NASA GIBS, WebCodecs with mp4-muxer (demo video), Vercel static hosting.

Use of SI: an SI (AI) assistant was used for research, writing and debugging code, documentation, and composing the demo video and slides, which are watermarked "SI-assisted". Every number is computed by deterministic code from NASA FIRMS data. No generated imagery is used. The demo narration is a synthetic AI voice (Microsoft Ava) and its music is generated in code.

Open source (MIT): github.com/su0as/firerelay, with the full pipeline, web app and validation results.
